```{r}
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)

UBSprices <- read.csv("http://aloy.rbind.io/data/UBSprices.csv")
bigmac.lm <- lm(bigmac2009 ~ bigmac2003, data = UBSprices)

florida <- read.csv(here("data", "florida_2000.csv"))
florida_lm <- lm(BUCHANAN ~ BUSH, data = florida)

bikes_mlr <- lm(rides ~ temp_actual * weekend, data = bikes)
```

## Regression is not resistant to outliers

Example from CS1. Solid line = fit with outliers included; dashed line = fit with outlier removed. One extreme county visibly "tilts" the line

```{r}
#| fig-height: 2
#| fig-width: 3
resid_df <- augment(florida_lm) |>
  mutate(outlier = .std.resid > 3)

gf_point(BUCHANAN ~ BUSH, data = filter(resid_df, outlier), shape = 17, color = "darkorange") |>
  gf_point(BUCHANAN ~ BUSH, data = filter(resid_df, !outlier), shape = 16) |>
  gf_lm(BUCHANAN ~ BUSH, data = resid_df, color = "darkorange") |>
  gf_lm(BUCHANAN ~ BUSH, data = resid_df[!resid_df$outlier, ], linetype = 2)
```

**Why SLR isn't resistant:**

$$\widehat\beta_1 = r \cdot \dfrac{s_y}{s_x} \quad \quad \quad \widehat\beta_0 = \bar y - \widehat\beta_1 \bar x$$


**MLR is no better**: we're still minimizing a *sum* of squared residuals and sums aren't resistant to outliers either.

$$SSE = \sum_{i=1}^n \left(y_i - (\widehat\beta_0 + \widehat\beta_1 x_{i1} + \cdots + \widehat\beta_p x_{ip})\right)^2$$

## Types of outliers

An observation can be unusual in $y$, in $x$, or both, and each type
pulls the fitted line differently. Below, one added point (orange)
plays each role against the same base cloud of points.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 2.5
#| fig-width: 8
set.seed(2013)
N <- 25
x <- rnorm(N)
y <- x + rnorm(N, sd = 0.5)
df <- tibble(x = x, y = y)
xnew <- c(0, 10, 10, 10)
ynew <- c(10, 0, predict(lm(y ~ x), newdata = list(x = 10)) + rnorm(1, sd = 0.5), 20)
labs4 <- c("Outlier in Y", "Outlier in X", "Outlier in X and Y\n(consistent w/ trend)", "Outlier in X and Y\n(extends trend)")

make_panel <- function(i) {
  df_out <- rbind(df, tibble(x = xnew[i], y = ynew[i]))
  gf_point(y ~ x, data = df, color = "black") |>
    gf_point(y ~ x, data = tibble(x = xnew[i], y = ynew[i]), color = "darkorange", size = 2) |>
    gf_lm(y ~ x, data = df, color = "black") |>
    gf_lm(y ~ x, data = df_out, color = "darkorange") |>
    gf_labs(title = labs4[i])
}

panels <- map(1:4, make_panel)
wrap_plots(panels, nrow = 1)
```

Points that are able to substantially change the fitted model are
called ________________. Not every outlier is influential -- an
outlier that falls *along* the existing trend barely moves the line
(panel 3 above), while one that breaks the trend can swing it a lot
(panels 1, 2, 4).

In higher dimensions, outliers can be tricky to spot -- detecting an
outlier in the predictor space means considering the multivariate
relationship *among all* predictors, not just one at a time.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-width: 9
ell1 <- gf_point(prestige ~ education, data = Duncan, ylab = "Y", xlab = "X1", title = "No outlier") +
  stat_ellipse(color = "blue", linetype = 2)
ell2 <- gf_point(prestige ~ income, data = Duncan, ylab = "Y", xlab = "X2", title = "Outlier in Y") +
  stat_ellipse(color = "blue", linetype = 2)
ell3 <- gf_point(income ~ education, data = Duncan, ylab = "X2", xlab = "X1", title = "Possible outlier in X") +
  stat_ellipse(color = "blue", linetype = 2)
ell1 | ell2 | ell3
```

How do we find outliers and decide if they're influential?

-   Plot the data
-   Plot the standardized residuals
-   Fit the model with and without the point(s)
-   Calculate *influence diagnostics* -- leverage, standardized
    residuals, DFFITS, Cook's distance

::: callout-tip
## Leverage (aka "hat")

Leverage measures a point's **potential to influence** the fitted
line, based only on _____________

For SLR: $h_i = \dfrac{1}{n} + \dfrac{(x_i - \bar x)^2}{\sum(x_i - \bar x)^2}$

For MLR: more complicated -- it's a distance of a case from the
average of all $p$ predictors.

"Flares up" when a point's $x$ is far from the mean, indicating
*potential* to be influential (whether it actually is depends on $y$
too).

**Cutoffs:** $2(p+1)/n$ or $3(p+1)/n$
:::

In higher dimensions, leverage is focusing on the distance from the average of all predictors.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-width: 9
duncan_lm <- lm(prestige ~ income + education, data = Duncan)
duncan_aug <- augment(duncan_lm) |>
  mutate(lev.flag = .hat > (2 * 3) / length(.hat))

le1 <- gf_point(prestige ~ education, data = duncan_aug, color = ~lev.flag) |>
  gf_refine(scale_color_manual(values = c("black", "darkorange")), theme(legend.position = "none")) |>
  gf_labs(x = "X1 (education)", y = "Y (prestige)")
le2 <- gf_point(prestige ~ income, data = duncan_aug, color = ~lev.flag) |>
  gf_refine(scale_color_manual(values = c("black", "darkorange")), theme(legend.position = "none")) |>
  gf_labs(x = "X2 (income)", y = "Y (prestige)")
le3 <- gf_point(income ~ education, data = duncan_aug, color = ~lev.flag) |>
  gf_hline(yintercept = mean(Duncan$income), linetype = 2) |>
  gf_vline(xintercept = mean(Duncan$education), linetype = 2) |>
  gf_refine(scale_color_manual(values = c("black", "darkorange")), theme(legend.position = "none")) |>
  gf_labs(x = "X1 (education)", y = "X2 (income)")

le1 | le2 | le3
```



::: callout-tip
## Standardized Residuals

Standardized residuals divide each residual by its standard deviation, which builds in a "penalty" for high-leverage points (a high-leverage point pulls the
line toward itself, shrinking its raw residual):

$$r_i = \frac{e_i}{\widehat\sigma\sqrt{1 - h_i}}$$

"Flares up" when $y_i$ is far from $\widehat y_i$.

**Cutoffs:** $|r_i| > 2$ for small data sets or $|r_i| > 4$ for large data sets

:::


::: callout-tip
## Cook's distance

**Cook's distance** measures the effect of case $i$ on **all** of the
fitted values at once:

$$D_i = \sum_{j=1}^n \frac{(\widehat y_{j(i)} - \widehat y_j)^2}{(p+1)\widehat\sigma^2} = \frac{r_i^2}{p+1}\left(\frac{h_i}{1-h_i}\right)$$

**Cutoff:** $D_i$ near or above ________ indicates large influence; also
worth comparing the *relative* size of $D_i$ across cases with an
index plot.

:::

## Doing this in R: `augment()`

We never calculate these by hand -- `broom::augment()` computes them
all for us:

-   `.hat`: leverage
-   `.std.resid`: standardized residuals
-   `.cooksd`: Cook's distance

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

augment(bikes_mlr)
```

```{r}
augment(bikes_mlr) |> select(-weekend) |> head(6) |> knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

## Shortcut for plots: `resid_panel()`

`ggResidpanel::resid_panel()` gives us residual, leverage, and Cook's
distance plots in one call:

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 2.5
#| echo: true


resid_panel(bigmac.lm, plots = c("resid", "lev", "cookd"), type = "standardized", nrow = 1)
```

What do we do if a case is influential?

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 5.5
graph TD
    %% Define the green color theme for all nodes
    classDef default fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px,color:#1b5e20;

    A(["Do the conclusions change <br> when the case is deleted?"])

    B["Proceed with the case in-<br>cluded. Study it to see if<br>anything can be learned."]

    C(["Is there reason to believe<br>the case belongs to a popu-<br>lation other than the one<br>under investigation?"])

    D["Omit the case and proceed."]

    E(["Does the case have unusu-<br>ally 'distant' explanatory<br>variable values?"])

    F["Omit the case and proceed.<br>Report conclusions for the<br>reduced range of explana-<br>tory variables."]

    G["Not much can be said. More<br>data (or clarification of the<br>influential case) are need-<br>ed to resolve the questions."]

    A -->|NO| B
    A -->|YES| C
    C -->|YES| D
    C -->|NO| E
    E -->|YES| F
    E -->|NO| G
```

*Source: Display 11.8 in* Sleuth *(3rd edition)*
